hints: Use the limewater test clue to identify the white solid residue, then think what two gases must come from $\text{Li}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 \cdot \text{H}_2\text{O}$ to leave that residue.
walkthrough:
Read the limewater clue**
A gas that turns limewater milky is $\text{CO}_2$. Here it comes from adding the white residue to $\text{HNO}_3(aq)$, so the residue itself must be a carbonate. For lithium that is $\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3$.

Balance what is left**
Start with $\text{Li}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O}$. If $\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3$ stays as solid, the remaining atoms are one C, one O plus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. That fits exactly $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ as one gaseous product and $\text{CO}$ as the other gaseous product.
Final answer: $\text{Li}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4\cdot\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}$

hints: Recall how decomposition temperature changes down Group 2 for nitrates and carbonates, and which cation is smaller out of $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$.
Link the smaller, more polarising cation to what it does to the large $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ anion to make decomposition easier.
walkthrough:
Recall the Group 2 stability pattern**
Think of Group 2 nitrates or carbonates. Stability increases down the group, so decomposition temperature increases down the group. Calcium compounds always decompose more easily than barium compounds.

Explain with polarisation**
Picture the $2+$ cation pulling on the electron cloud of the $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ anion. $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ with the same charge, so it has higher charge density and greater polarising power. It distorts the anion more, weakens the C-C and C-O bonds inside it, so less heat is needed to break it apart.

Final answer: $\text{CaC}_2\text{O}_4$ decomposes at the lower temperature.
$\text{Ca}^{2+}$ has a smaller ionic radius / higher charge density than $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, so it more strongly polarises / distorts the $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ anion, weakening bonds within the anion.

hints: Think what happens to the five 3d orbitals when ligands approach a transition metal ion, are they still all the same energy?
Consider what an electron in a lower d orbital can do if it absorbs exactly the right amount of energy from visible light.
Remember the colour you see is not the colour absorbed, so what is the relationship between absorbed light and transmitted colour?
walkthrough:
Split the d orbitals**
In a free $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ion the five 3d orbitals have the same energy. When six oxygen atoms from three ethanedioate ligands surround it octahedrally, lone pairs repel d electrons unequally. Some d orbitals point directly at ligands and are raised in energy, others point between and stay lower. This is d-orbital splitting.

Promote an electron with light**
Because the gap between the lower and higher d sets matches the energy of visible light photons, an electron can absorb a photon and jump up. This is a d-d transition. Only a partially filled d subshell can do this, which is why transition metals show it.

Link absorption to observed green**
If red light is absorbed to provide that jump energy, red is removed from white light. Your eye sees everything that is left, which is the complementary colour. For this complex the combination transmitted gives the green solution observed.

Final answer: Ligands cause splitting of the d orbitals into orbitals of different energy.
Electrons are promoted / excited from a lower energy d orbital to a higher energy d orbital by absorbing visible light.
The colour observed is the complementary colour to the light absorbed.

hints: Count Fe, K, $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$ and $\text{CO}_2$ on each side and try doubling $\text{K}_3[\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]$ to balance Fe and K first.
walkthrough:
Balance by inspection**
You need the same number of Fe on both sides. One $\text{K}_2[\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_2]$ contains one Fe, so start with 2 on the left to match 2 on the right. That gives 6 K on the left, which fits $2 \times \text{K}_2$ plus $1 \times \text{K}_2$ on the right. Carbon and oxygen then balance with $2\text{CO}_2$ from oxidation of one ethanedioate. Fe(III) is reduced to Fe(II) while ethanedioate is oxidised.
Final answer: $2\text{K}_3\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3 \rightarrow 2\text{K}_2\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_2 + \text{K}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 + 2\text{CO}_2$

hints: Remember $[\text{Fe}(\text{C}_2\text{O}_4)_3]^{3-}$ has three bidentate ligands around octahedral Fe, so no cis-trans isomerism is possible, only a propeller twist.
Think how to draw the second isomer from the first, what symmetry operation relates a pair of optical isomers?
walkthrough:
Draw one propeller**
Place Fe in the centre with octahedral geometry. Add three $\text{O-O}$ arcs, each arc is one $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ chelating through two O atoms. Use a vertical line for one chelate in the plane, one wedge pair coming out and one dashed pair going back to show 3D. This creates a left handed or right handed propeller.

Draw the mirror image**
Now draw the exact mirror reflection of that propeller. Swap every wedge to dash and every dash to wedge. The two structures cannot be superimposed by rotation, so they are a pair of optical isomers / enantiomers. No plane of symmetry exists.

Final answer: Two 3D structures of octahedral Fe with three $\text{O-O}$ bidentate oxalate chelates arranged as a propeller.
Isomer 1 and isomer 2 are non-superimposable mirror images (delta and lambda enantiomers), drawn with wedges / solid lines for bonds out of the plane and hatched / dashed lines for bonds into the plane.

hints: For added acid, think how $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-$ can act as a base to remove $\text{H}^+$.
For added alkali, think how $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-$ can act as an acid to remove $\text{OH}^-$ and form water.
walkthrough:
Remove added H+**
$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-$ is the conjugate base of ethanedioic acid, so it can accept a proton. When acid is added, $\text{H}^+$ is mopped up: $$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$$ This prevents a large fall in pH.

Remove added OH-**
$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^-$ still has one acidic proton, so it can donate it to alkali. When alkali is added, $\text{OH}^-$ is mopped up: $$\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ This prevents a large rise in pH.

Final answer: With acid: $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$
With alkali: $\text{HC}_2\text{O}_4^- + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Identify which half equation is reduction (more positive $E^\ominus$) and which must be reversed as oxidation, then balance electrons to 4e-.
Recall $E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{cathode} - E^\ominus_{anode}$ using the given reduction potentials without changing them for stoichiometry.
walkthrough:
Combine to get the overall reaction**
The $\text{O}_2 / \text{OH}^-$ equation with $E^\ominus = +0.40\ \text{V}$ is the cathode reduction. The $\text{CO}_2 / \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ equation with $E^\ominus = -0.59\ \text{V}$ must run backwards as oxidation at the anode. Multiply the second equation by 2 to give $4e^-$ to match the first: $$2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} \rightarrow 4\text{CO}_2 + 4e^-$$ Add to $$\text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) + 4e^- \rightarrow 4\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$$ Electrons cancel to give $$2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) \rightarrow 4\text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$$

Calculate Ecell**
Use reduction potentials directly: $$E^\ominus_{cell} = E^\ominus_{cathode} - E^\ominus_{anode}$$ $$E^\ominus_{cell} = 0.40 - (-0.59) = +0.99\ \text{V}$$ The positive value shows the fuel cell reaction is feasible.

Final answer: overall: $2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l}) \rightarrow 4\text{CO}_2(\text{g}) + 4\text{OH}^-(\text{aq})$
$E^\ominus_{cell} = 0.40 - (-0.59) = +0.99\ \text{V}$
